$comment: SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH -- EDIT THIS FILE.

The ID registry: what every row-ID prefix of the documentation MEANS, and where its rows are defined. The keys are the ID registry keys of the NDD review standard, appendix A.6 'List of JSON Keys': `prefix`, `standsFor` (the English words the letters stand for), `meaning` (one line saying what the numbered rows index, per BCP 47 language tag; `en` is the master) and `section` (the one place that defines the rows: a table id, the UID an untitled table stands under, or a ledger or rules file). Every key the project adds starts with `x`: `xOwner` is the tree that DEFINES the rows, `xMirroredIn` names a tree that only RECORDS them, `xPending` marks a prefix registered before its rows exist, and the top-level `xCollisionsSuppressed` lists the collisions held open. row-id-prefixes.schema.json holds the shape.
Rebuild: npm run gen   |   npm run gen:check fails if anything has drifted.

THIS FILE HOLDS NO ROSTER. Which prefixes exist, every table each is defined in and how many rows it has are read on every run from FOUR trees -- docs/spec, docs/development-records, docs/development-rules and docs/review -- as every `| XX-n |` row of their Markdown and the table caption it sits under. Do NOT write a row count or a list of tables here: the join between this file and that walk IS the check, and a copy of either side would be the thing that drifts. A prefix a tree uses and this file does not carry fails the run (unregistered); a prefix this file carries and no tree uses fails it too (dead registration). There is no separate checker. docs/review is SCOPED: only the prefixes this file gives it (xOwner or xMirroredIn `review`, today RVF, the review findings of rule 07) are counted there, because its working notes number their rows ad hoc.

`section` IS A CLAIM THE GENERATOR TESTS. The standard requires it, so the file names ONE home of the rows, and the walk must find the owner tree defining rows of the prefix there; a table renumbered or moved without this file fails the run instead of drifting in silence. The walk still prints every table and counts the rows.

THE WALK COVERS SEVERAL TREES BECAUSE THE DEFECT IT EXISTS FOR SPANS THEM. One prefix can name a row of the specification and a row of the ledger, and a register that walked only docs/spec could not see the second one.

`xMirroredIn` IS A CLAIM THE GENERATOR TESTS, not a way to silence it. A mirror is a tree that records work about rows the owner defines (the ledger's UF-32 is the specification's UF-32), so the generator holds every id in the mirroring tree against the ids the owner defines and fails on the first one the owner never wrote. That test is what separates the real mirrors from the prefixes that mean two different things. `xCollisionsSuppressed` is empty: no prefix stands in two trees with two meanings.

`xCollisionsSuppressed` IS A DEBT, NOT A PERMISSION. Each entry names the prefix, the trees it is used in, the day the suppression was written, why, and what removes it. The printed table shows every one of them, so the count cannot grow in silence, and the generator fails on an entry whose prefix no longer collides -- a suppression cannot outlive its reason.

`standsFor` MAY BE EMPTY, and an empty one is not a gap to be filled by guessing. It says the letters' origin could not be read out of the documents themselves. The defect this registry exists to remove is a spelling that two readers expand two ways, so an invented expansion here would be that same defect with a registry around it. Write `meaning` and leave `standsFor` empty.

`xPending: true` SUPPRESSES THE DEAD-REGISTRATION ERROR, and only that. It is for a prefix registered ahead of the wave that writes its rows; such an entry writes an empty `section`, and the printed table shows it as a registration with no rows yet, so a reader can see what is suppressed and count it. The generator faults a pending prefix that HAS rows, so the flag cannot outlive its reason.

`meaning` holds `en` and `ja`. English is the master (NDD review standard, appendix A.6); the specification prints the `ja` text because it is a Japanese document. `standsFor` is Latin letters and belongs to no language.
